analysis.one_liner: Requires large multinational companies to publicly report their profits and taxes country by country.
analysis.headline: The bill, introduced in July 2026 with one cosponsor, has sat in the House Financial Services Committee since the day it was introduced, with no hearing, markup, or vote.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would amend securities law to require large multinational companies that file with the SEC to disclose, on a country-by-country basis, where they book their revenues, profits, employees, and assets, and how much income tax they actually pay in each place, including tax havens. The data would be published online in a machine-readable public format. The point is to make offshore profit-shifting visible to investors, journalists, and tax enforcers instead of buried in global totals.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary taxpayers, who effectively cover the gap when corporations shift profits to low-tax jurisdictions; small domestic businesses that compete against multinationals using offshore structures; investors and journalists who currently cannot see where a company's profits sit versus where its real activity is; and tax authorities, who gain a public roadmap of profit-shifting. Companies that pay taxes where they operate also benefit from a more level field.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Taxpayers and domestic businesses competing against offshore profit-shifting

how_it_helps.text: Covered issuers — companies in multinational groups above a revenue threshold set by the SEC — must file a report listing every subsidiary, its tax jurisdiction of residence and incorporation, and for each jurisdiction the revenues from and outside related-party dealings, pre-tax profit, cash income taxes paid, accrued tax expense, stated capital, accumulated earnings, employee headcount, and tangible assets. [S2] [S1]

The definition of a tax jurisdiction explicitly includes non-country jurisdictions with fiscal autonomy, which captures tax havens and territories, so shifting profits to a haven is disclosed jurisdiction by jurisdiction rather than hidden in a worldwide total. [S2]

The reports must be filed in a machine-readable format prescribed by the SEC and made available to the public online, meaning anyone — not just regulators — can compare where a company books profit against where it pays tax. [S2]
The SEC must issue a proposed rule within 270 days of enactment and a final rule within one year, with the requirement taking effect one year after the final rule. [S2]
Filing is due on the deadline for the company's tax return, so the public disclosure is aligned with actual tax payments rather than an accounting construct. [S2]

analysis.who_pays: Large multinational companies, which bear the compliance cost of building and publishing jurisdiction-level data, and which lose the obscurity that currently lets profits booked in tax havens go unexamined. Compliance-intensive multinationals that compete against foreign firms facing lighter disclosure may also argue for a relative cost.

drawbacks.text: Covered companies must collect and report jurisdiction-level data for every subsidiary within a fixed rulemaking timeline, a real compliance cost particularly for complex multinational groups. [S2]

A common objection to public country-by-country reporting is that pre-tax profit does not always line up cleanly with a single jurisdiction's activity, so the published numbers could be read as evidence of tax avoidance where complex group structures, not haven-shifting, explain the figures. [S2]

US-headquartered multinationals would face public tax-geography disclosure that many foreign competitors do not face under their home rules, which critics argue disadvantages them; the bill's conform-to-US-or-international-standards language does not require other countries to match the publicity. [S2]

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit to the public is significant but indirect: disclosure does not by itself change tax law or collect a dollar, but it gives investors, journalists, and tax enforcers the map of profit-shifting that currently does not exist, and it is cheap for the public because companies already must compute much of this data for existing country-by-country tax reporting — the change is making it public rather than confidential. The costs are real compliance burdens for multinationals and a plausible competitive-symmetry argument, but those costs fall on the entities whose conduct the bill is meant to expose. On balance the design is straightforward and the bill's main weakness is not its content but its lack of support.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and sent to the House Financial Services Committee the same day, and nothing has happened to it since — no hearing, no markup, no vote.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced in the House on July 16, 2026, by Rep. Brittany Pettersen with Del. Eleanor Holmes Norton as an original cosponsor. [S1] [S2]

It was referred to the House Committee on Financial Services on the day of introduction, and the full action history shows no further action — no hearing, markup, committee vote, or floor action. [S4] [S1]
It has one cosponsor, Del. Norton of DC, and no Republican support on the sponsor or cosponsor list. [S3] [S1]
The 119th Congress runs through January 3, 2027, so the bill is technically alive but has only a short window in which a committee that has taken no action on it would need to move it. [S1]

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Multinationals that shift profits to tax havens are better off for now, since the disclosure that would expose where they book profits and pay taxes has not advanced, and no comparable public reporting requirement has taken its place. Ordinary taxpayers and domestic competitors gain nothing from the bill's inaction.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Multinationals keeping profit-shifting out of public view

industries.industry: Multinational corporations that shift profits to tax havens
industries.note: The bill would force public, jurisdiction-level disclosure of where these companies book profits, pay taxes, and employ people, ending the obscurity that makes haven-shifting invisible in public filings. The industry's interest in keeping this data confidential runs directly against the public's interest in seeing it. [S2]

industries.industry: Offshore financial and tax-haven services (jurisdictions with fiscal autonomy and the service firms that route profits through them)
industries.note: The bill's definition of tax jurisdiction explicitly covers non-country jurisdictions with fiscal autonomy, so the flows that pass through these structures would be individually visible rather than aggregated. Public scrutiny of those flows tends to shrink demand for them. [S2]

Covered companies would need to produce jurisdiction-level reports in a machine-readable SEC-prescribed format on tax-return deadlines, creating compliance work, though much of the underlying data already exists for confidential tax country-by-country reporting. [S2]

analysis.trajectory: With roughly two and a half months left in the 119th Congress, a single sponsor, one cosponsor, and a committee that has taken no action in the months since referral, the most likely path is that the bill expires at the end of this Congress without a hearing or a vote; the sponsor could reintroduce it in the next Congress.
